explanations.explanation: Consolation is the word. Job says, “…let this be your consolation to me.” I think he's asking for the one comfort that costs his friends nothing, and that's open ears. Listening is a gift you can give without even standing up, friend. A warm pair of ears beats a cold cookie any day.

I see why you'd say burden, because Job sounds like a man carrying a lot. But he says their listening would be their “consolation” to him. He's asking them to give comfort, not to pile on more weight. Listening is the easy part of comforting, and even I can do it, and I'm mostly mustache.

A warning would come with a pointed finger, and Job isn't pointing at anybody here. He says, “…let this be your consolation to me.” That's a request for comfort, plain and simple. I think he just wants his friends to sit still and hear him out.

explanations.answer: Be appalled and cover their mouths
explanations.explanation: That's it. Job says, “Look at me and be appalled; put your hand over your mouth.” He wants his friends to really see him, and then to stop talking. I think he's tired of speeches, friend. Hands over mouths is the quietest advice in the whole chapter.

explanations.answer: Be still and lift up their eyes
explanations.explanation: Close, because Job does want their eyes on him. But he says “Look at me,” not lift up your eyes, and he says “be appalled,” not be still. Then the hand goes over their own mouth. That's a gasp-and-hush kind of moment, not a calm one.

explanations.answer: Be brave and take hold of his hand
explanations.explanation: It sounds sweet, but nobody grabs anybody's hand in this verse. The only hand mentioned is the one the friends are told to put “over your mouth.” Job doesn't say a word about being brave, either. I think he's asking for a stunned silence, not a hug.

explanations.answer: Why do the wicked live on
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. Job asks, “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” Zophar, one of Job's friends, talked about how short the wicked man's triumph is (Job 20:5). Job turns around and asks why the wicked keep going. That's a head-on collision, friend.

explanations.answer: Why do the wicked never rest
explanations.explanation: Never resting is the opposite of what Job describes. He says they “spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace” (Job 21:13). That's a pretty restful picture. His question is about why they live on and grow in power.

explanations.answer: Why do the wicked fear death
explanations.explanation: Fear isn't in this picture at all. Job says their homes are “safe from fear” (Job 21:9). His question is “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” He's puzzled about their long, strong lives, not their worries.

Yes, punishment. Job says their homes are safe from fear, and “no rod of punishment from God is upon them.” A rod is what comes down when you've got it coming, and Job says it isn't coming down on their houses. That's the part that has him so troubled.

Job does talk about how well things go for the wicked, so I get the pull of this one. But the verse says “no rod of punishment from God is upon them.” A rod is something that strikes, and Job says there isn't one. He's describing what's missing, not something handed out.

Comfort fits the cozy picture, with safe homes and no fear. But the word in this verse is “punishment.” Job says “no rod of punishment from God is upon them.” The rod is the thing that never shows up at their door.

explanations.answer: Skipping about and singing to music
explanations.explanation: You got the party. Job says “…their children skip about, singing to the tambourine and lyre and making merry at the sound of the flute.” That's a full band, friend, with tambourine, lyre and flute. It's the picture of a happy, carefree house.

explanations.answer: Working in the fields beside their fathers
explanations.explanation: No fields in this scene. Job says the children “skip about, singing to the tambourine and lyre.” They're making merry at the sound of the flute. That's a lot more party than payday.

explanations.answer: Sitting quietly by the city gate
explanations.explanation: Quiet is the one thing this scene isn't. Job describes children who “skip about, singing to the tambourine and lyre and making merry at the sound of the flute.” No gate is mentioned. With that many instruments, nobody's whispering.

Terror isn't what Job says. He says the wicked “spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace.” Sheol is the place of the dead. So their ending, in Job's words, is peaceful, and that's exactly what troubles him.

False is right. Job says the wicked “spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace.” Sheol is the place of the dead. He says peace, not terror, and that peace is what he's wrestling with.

That's true. Job is quoting what the wicked say to God: “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him?” Notice they're asking what's in it for them. They want to know the payoff before they'll pray. I think that's a pretty cold way to talk to Someone who gives so much.

The text says otherwise. Right after “Leave us alone!” the wicked ask, “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him, and what would we gain if we pray to Him?” So Job does report that they ask what they would gain from praying. Pay attention to who is talking there, friend. It's the wicked, and Job is quoting them.

Yes. Job says, “…so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked.” He just described how well things go for them, and still he keeps his distance. He says their prosperity “is not in their own hands.” I think that's a man with his feet planted, friend.
Job isn't putting their advice on a scale. He says, “…I stay far from the counsel of the wicked.” Far means far. There's no weighing, no considering, just distance.
No sneaking around here. Job says, “…I stay far from the counsel of the wicked.” Nothing in the verse hints at secret following. He says it out loud, and that's the opposite of sneaking.

Straw and chaff it is. Job asks, “Are they like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away by a storm?” Both are light, dry bits that a gust can carry off. He's asking whether that really happens to the wicked, and from what he just said, the picture doesn't match what he sees.

Grass and flowers are a nice picture, but they're not what Job names here. He asks, “Are they like straw before the wind, like chaff swept away by a storm?” Straw and chaff are the two things in his question. Easy to mix up when the wind's blowing, friend.

Smoke and mist vanish in a puff, so I see why it came to mind. But Job's words are “straw before the wind” and “chaff swept away by a storm.” Those are the two things he names. Smoke never gets a mention.

Repay is the word. Job says, “Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it.” He's answering the saying that punishment is laid up for a man's children. Job wants the man himself to be the one who knows it. In the next verses he says, “For what does he care about his household after him…”

Forgiveness is a beautiful thing, but it's not what Job asks for here. He says, “Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it.” The man in question is the one who did it. Job wants that man himself to know it.

A warning would come before something happens, but Job is asking about what comes after. He says, “Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it.” Repay is the word, friend. The weight lands on the man, and not on his children.

Nobody can. Job asks, “Can anyone teach knowledge to God, since He judges those on high?” I think the way he asks it, he expects the answer to be no one. God is the One who judges even those on high, so no teacher stands above Him. It's a humbling question, friend.

That's a kind guess, but Job doesn't carve out a spot for the wise. He asks, “Can anyone teach knowledge to God, since He judges those on high?” I think the question points to no one. Even a very wise person has nothing to add to the One who judges those on high.
Age isn't what Job has in mind. He asks, “Can anyone teach knowledge to God, since He judges those on high?” I think he expects the answer no one. Gray hair doesn't change that, friend.

Bitterness is it. Job says this other man “dies in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity.” It's a heavy picture, a life that never got a taste of the good stuff. I think Job wants his friends to feel the difference between these two men.

Peace belongs to the first man, who dies “completely secure and at ease.” The second man dies “in the bitterness of his soul.” Job lines them up on purpose, one ending easy and one ending hard. This is a heavy part, friend.

Strength goes with the first man, who dies “full of vigor.” The second man's ending is different. He dies “in the bitterness of his soul, having never tasted prosperity.” It's a heavy contrast, and Job means for it to sting.

It doesn't work that way in Job's words. He says, “But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.” Both men end up in the same place, the one who had plenty and the one who had nothing. This is a heavy picture, and it isn't only about the bitter one.

False is right. Job says, “But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both.” The man who had it all and the man who never tasted prosperity end up in the same place. It's a sober point, and Job makes it plainly.

Travelers are the answer. Job asks, “Have you never asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their reports?” People on the road have seen other towns and other houses. So Job sends his friends to ask folks who've seen more than one neighborhood.

Elders at the gate are a fine source in general, but they aren't the ones Job names. He asks about “those who travel the roads.” The reports he wants his friends to accept come from people who've been out and about. The gate never comes up, friend.

Priests aren't in this verse. Job asks his friends, “Have you never asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their reports?” The ones he points to are people on the road. Altars stay out of it.

True. Job says, “Indeed, the evil man is spared from the day of calamity, delivered from the day of wrath.” That's what he reports, and it's the opposite of what his friends keep insisting. It's the same puzzle he's been chewing on all chapter, friend.

The text says the opposite. Job states, “Indeed, the evil man is spared from the day of calamity, delivered from the day of wrath.” Spared is the word he uses. Job isn't saying the evil man gets hit, and that's exactly why he's so troubled.

explanations.answer: He is carried to the grave and his tomb is watched
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Job says, “He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb.” This is a man given a careful send-off, not a quick one. Job's point is that nobody stops him on the way. It's a heavy part, so I'll let it sit.

explanations.answer: He is thrown outside the city and left unburied
explanations.explanation: Job says nothing like that. He says, “He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb.” That's a burial with care, and not a tossing out. I think that's what makes it hard for Job to understand.

explanations.answer: He is buried in a hurry and quickly forgotten
explanations.explanation: Job paints the opposite picture. He says, “He is carried to the grave, and watch is kept over his tomb.” He adds that “everyone follows behind him.” That's no rushed goodbye, friend, and nobody in this scene is hurrying off.

Falsehood is the word, and it's sharp. Job says, “So how can you comfort me with empty words? For your answers remain full of falsehood.” That's about as direct as a man can be. Think of a cookie box with a fancy bow and nothing inside, friend.

Wisdom would be a compliment, and Job isn't handing out compliments right now. He says their answers “remain full of falsehood.” He calls their comfort “empty words.” I think he's hurting and has run out of patience.

Kindness would be nice to hear, but that's not what Job says. He calls their comfort “empty words” and says their answers “remain full of falsehood.” Those are strong words from a hurting man. I think he wished his friends had given him something real.
